blocks.text: I shall only observe that the Hebrews were so ignorant of what kind of animal the chameleon is that they took it to be a bird. My witness is Kimchi, who, inquiring in his Lexicon what לילית lilith is, Es. XXXIV, 14., writes that some assert שהוא עוף גדל מן הרוח כמו סלמנדרא מן האש שקורין לו קמליאן that Lilith is a bird which feeds on air (as the salamander on fire), which they call the chameleon. Of the same kind is the description of the salamander in the Tanchuma, section וישב, fol. 18. a., as similar to a spider. The words run thus: When glassmakers, who make glass, have kept the furnace burning for seven days and 7 nights without interruption, from the force of the fire היוצא משם בריה הדומה לעכבית והבריה קורין אותה סלמנדרא there comes forth an animal similar to a spider, which animal is called the salamander. Some would read לעכבר, to a mouse, instead of לעכבית, to a spider; but this is no sounder, since the salamander is no more like a mouse than like a spider. Since, then, the nature of animals was so little understood by the Hebrews, they are not to be trusted rashly in explaining these words.

[II, 509] In the Greek version it is said of Nineveh, Soph. II, 4.: χαμαιλέοντες, καὶ ἐχῖνοι ἐν τοῖς φατνώμασιν αὐτῆς κοιταθήσονται [chamaileontes, kai echinoi en tois phatnōmasin autēs koitathēsontai]; Chameleons and hedgehogs shall lie in its coffered ceilings. But in the Hebrew text, in place of the chameleon, there is קאת, which the same translators render pelican in Levit. XI, 18. and Ps. CI, (Hebr. CII,) 7. Why, then, is the same word taken here for the chameleon? If, with the Complutensian editors, we write λέοντες [leontes] for χαμαιλέοντες [chamaileontes], we shall not cure the fault, because the Hebrew קאת no more means lion than chameleon. I suspect that the Greeks read לטאה in place of קאת, a kind of lizard, which for them in Leviticus is καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], stellio [gecko], and here would have been χαμαιλέων [chamaileōn], since these species are not infrequently confused; or else that καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], or, what is the same, γαλεώτης [galeōtēs], was changed into χαμαιλέοντες [chamaileontes] ^{(5)}. In support of this is the fact that the chameleon is nowhere said to lie ἐν τοῖς φατνώμασιν [en tois phatnōmasin], in coffered ceilings. But this is characteristic of the καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], or γαλεώτης [galeōtēs], the stellio. Hence Dioscorides, book 6, chapter 1, directs that food be prepared in the open air; or, if it is prepared ἐν ὑποστέγῳ [en hypostegō], in a covered place, ἐπιμελῶς καταμανθάνειν τὰς ὀροφὰς, πολλάκις γὰρ ἐκ τῶν ὑπερκειμένων πίπτει ζωΰφια φθοροποιὰ, ὥσπερ φαλάγγια, καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ ἑρπετὰ, καὶ ὁ καλούμενος ἀσκαλαβώτης [epimelōs katamanthanein tas orophas, pollakis gar ek tōn hyperkeimenōn piptei zōyphia phthoropoia, hōsper phalangia, kai alla tina herpeta, kai ho kaloumenos askalabōtēs], to examine carefully the vault of the roof, or the coffered ceiling (if you prefer): for deadly little creatures often fall from above, such as spiders and certain other reptiles, and the one called the stellio. And in the Clouds of Aristophanes, Act 1, it is said of Socrates:

Ζητοῦντες αὐτοῦ τῆς σελήνης τὰς ὁδοὺς, [col. 1083] Καὶ τὰς περιφορὰς, εἶτ᾽ ἄνω κεχηνότος, Ἀπὸ τῆς ὀροφῆς νύκτωρ γαλεώτης κατέχεσεν· [Zētountes autou tēs selēnēs tas hodous, kai tas periphoras, eit᾽ anō kechēnotos, apo tēs orophēs nyktōr galeōtēs katechesen]

As he was investigating the paths and revolutions of the moon, and gaping upward, a stellio from the ceiling of the roof dropped its excrement on him at night. Some take τὰ φατνώματα [ta phatnōmata] to be mangers. I see that the translators of the Greek text were in this very ridiculous error. Yet even if you follow them, you will gain nothing, because the stellio is accustomed to frequent mangers as much as the coffered ceilings of roofs. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 1: Κωλωτῇ δ᾽ ὄνος πολέμιος. Κοιμᾶται γὰρ ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ αὐτῆς, καὶ κωλύει ἐθίειν, εἰς τοὺς μυκτῆρας ἐνδυόμενος· [Kōlōtē d᾽ onos polemios. Koimatai gar en tē phatnē autēs, kai kōlyei ethiein, eis tous myktēras endyomenos] The ass is an enemy to the stellio. For the stellio sleeps in its manger and, entering its nostrils, prevents it from eating. Whereas the chameleon lives in desert places. But more will be said about the stellio in the following chapter.
